results.title: Two Divorces, Ten Children And A $2 Billion Fortune: Meet The Utah Couple Behind An E-Commerce Empire
results.author:
Alicia Park, Forbes Staff, 
 Alicia Park, Forbes Staff
 https://www.forbes.com/sites/aliciapark/
results.content:
On September 19 last year, the husband-and-wife cofounders of e-commerce company Pattern, David Wright and Melanie Alder, walked up together to the NASDAQ podium in Times Square—both dressed in black button-up shirts and custom blue and purple Nike Air Forces. Wright, CEO of the Lehi, Utah-based company, took the microphone to thank the room full of employees. “Mel and I get asked, ‘How did you do it?’ We didn’t…it’s a team sport,” Wright exclaimed as he took off his shoe, eagerly holding it up to the crowd.
It was a surreal moment for Wright and Alder: Ringing the NASDAQ bell was something they’d never imagined when they first began reselling fridge magnets on Amazon out of Alder’s living room in 2013. “We were just trying to bring in a little extra money on the side,” Wright explains from a conference room overlooking Utah’s sprawling mountainscape from Pattern’s headquarters in the tech hub known as Silicon Slopes. “Yeah, in the beginning, it was just us trying to support our families,” Alder chimes in from the seat next to his. At the time, both were married to other people: Alder was raising four children with her now ex-husband, while Wright had six of his own with his now ex-wife.
Money is no longer a concern. Since its September IPO, Pattern’s stock price has nearly doubled, with a four-month long surge starting in March pushing the company’s market cap above $4 billion. In July, when Pattern’s stock hit a record high of $29, CEO Wright’s net worth reached $1.7 billion and chief strategy officer Alder’s climbed to $1.1 billion. Though Pattern’s stock has dropped since, the couple, who together own 55% of the company, have a combined $2.2 billion stake as of August 7, plus nearly $90 million in cash from selling some of their shares shortly after the IPO. The now married couple, who tied the knot in 2018, share 10 kids between them—including two, Wright’s daughter and Alder’s son, who began dating soon after their parents’ wedding and are now married.
The core of Pattern’s business is to relieve consumer brands of the major headache that comes with trying to figure out the lucrative but overly complicated online marketplaces such as Amazon, says Scott Needham, a former reseller and founder of Amazon market research firm SmartScout. Pattern buys a brand’s products in bulk, handles the entire selling process from setting up online storefronts to delivery logistics and profits from selling the products at a markup across more than 70 marketplaces including Amazon, TikTok Shop, Walmart and Korean shopping mall Coupang. Over the years, Pattern has added complementary technology services, using data science and AI to help more than 200 brands—including Panasonic, SkullCandy and Spanx—more effectively sell their products.
For instance, mouthwash brand SmartMouth was seeing only a handful of Amazon sales when it enlisted Pattern to help. Pattern was able to track pricing data across every mouthwash product listed on Amazon, then recommend a new price low enough to better position SmartMouth against competitors without cutting into profit. Its AI software, which was fed images and videos of SmartMouth's mouthwashes, automated multiple ad campaigns and wrote up product descriptions that were tailored to boost the product in search rankings—based on data from competitor ads and storefronts, as well as a trove of internal data Pattern was sitting on thanks to its decade-long experience selling on Amazon. Three years later, SmartMouth says Amazon is its largest sales channel.
That playbook has helped fuel revenue growth of more than 40% every quarter since Pattern went public. Revenue hit $2.5 billion last year, up 39% from 2024, and the company has already brought in $1.6 billion in the first half of 2026. But hefty expenses from buying up all that inventory and handling shipping and returns for retailers makes Pattern's financials look more like a clothing or restaurant business than a hot tech company: Last year's net profit totaled just $16 million, largely due to one-time expenses from going public. For the first half of 2026, net profit was a still modest 3% of its revenue at $56 million.
Despite the capital-intensive nature of the business, Pattern has beat earnings expectations every quarter and is slowly putting its name on the map. That’s helped the little-known company garner interest from public market investors and double its stock price since March, multiple software analysts told Forbes. The six month lock-up period, during which employees or private investors cannot sell their shares after a company goes public, also ended in March—after which there were more shares available for public investors to buy.
The stock surge been enough to anoint Pattern as one of the most valuable companies in Utah’s picturesque Silicon Slopes, most notably home to tech companies including survey analytics software Qualtrics (acquired for $12.5 billion in 2023) and DNA testing service Ancestry.com (acquired for $4.7 billion in 2020). And if Wright has his way, Pattern will one day be the state’s most valuable company.
Wright grew up in Utah with five siblings—his dad was a land appraiser; his mom, an elementary school teacher. Alder was raised in Nevada with seven siblings. Her dad supported the entire family on a government job that paid just $45,000 a year, while her mom stayed home with the kids. Both Wright and Alder went on to attend Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah and crossed paths at different points in their lives, but never formally met until Alder’s then-husband Scott Keate introduced them to each other. Keate had known Wright for years: the childhood neighbors grew up two houses away from each other, both attended BYU and worked at the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints during an overlapping time. “Scott was someone that Dave looked up to. I think Scott was a year older than Dave, and Scott was a big star on the cross-country team growing up. And Dave was kind of in awe of him,” says a source who knew them both.
Around 2011, the two families were pursuing real estate side hustles when Keate heard Wright was looking for someone to help sell some of his properties, so Keate introduced Wright to his then-wife Alder. Over the next few years, Wright got to see her in action. “If something would hit the market, she was standing at the property when they were putting the key on the door,” Wright recalls. “She just had a way about her where she would talk people into giving her anything she wanted.”
So when Wright heard his cousin’s wife made $2 million from reselling children’s headbands online, he couldn’t think of anyone better than Alder to run the operations for a similar business he wanted to set up. Over lunch in January 2013, Alder—who stayed at home with the kids while then-husband Keate worked full-time as a consulting manager at Adobe—agreed and got to work immediately.
They started with fridge magnets, but soon expanded to supplements, lotions, essential oils—anything they could get their hands on. Everything was delivered in bulk to Alder’s home, then packaged and shipped out from her living room. She ran the day-to-day operations, while Wright would chip in—mainly on the tech side—after working his day job as a data analyst at the Church. “I didn't dare quit my job. I didn’t know if it would work,” Wright says. “She ran it from 2013 to 2015—which, if we’re being honest, (those first two years) are when companies survive or die.”
B y 2015, the business, then called iServe, started taking off and signed its first contract to be the exclusive reseller to health supplement maker Thorne. The business also became dependably profitable—enough for the cofounders to take home their first paychecks—so Wright and his coworker Jason Wells, who became chief technology officer, quit their jobs to work on iServe full time. It was that year that Wright and Alder began spending noticeably more time with each other, Alder’s ex-husband Keate recalls.
It was also that year Alder and Wright say they both separately began considering divorces from their spouses, claiming they were not happy in their marriages for reasons unrelated to each other. However, Keate alleges Alder admitted to him in 2015 that she had started developing feelings for Wright. Keate says that though he does not think Wright and Alder established a formal romantic relationship prior to the divorces, the cofounders’ close relationship was a factor for him in the separation. Wright’s former wife declined to comment.
Alder, who left the Church in 2009 after growing up Mormon, says it was only after Wright left the Church that she started considering a relationship with him. Wright, who left the Church shortly after his divorce in 2016, says he mustered up the courage to ask Alder out to dinner for their first date in late 2016.“You're taking two data-crazed fanatics and you start combining that with religion and it opens up enough questions that I guess we just sort of fell off that train,” Wright says. “Truthfully, I think that's when the door opened for a relationship,” Alder adds. “I consider that something really important to align on.”
Less than two years after their first date, in early 2018, the cofounders got married. That same year, they also renamed their business from iServe to Pattern, opened a corporate headquarters in Utah’s Silicon Slopes and began setting up warehouses outside of Utah as they began aggressively expanding.
A fter seven years of bootstrapping the business, Pattern raised its first outside investment in 2020 across two funding rounds totaling $277 million, giving the company a $2 billion valuation at the time. The new capital was used for acquisitions, international expansion and hiring new talent as demand for their services grew. By the end of 2022, Pattern had 1,400 employees, two new offices in Singapore and India and $1 billion in annual sales.
But the company’s rapid growth came with challenges. In 2022, the founder of a skincare business that Pattern had acquired as part of a new business strategy in 2020 filed a lawsuit alleging sexist behavior from male superiors to female employees on his team. Pattern denied the claims and countersued, alleging the founder had lied about his business’ profitability to Pattern prior to the acquisition. A Pattern spokesperson told Forbes the lawsuit and countersuit between Pattern and the founder were settled in 2024 with no admission of wrongdoing from either party.
Though the lawsuits were settled, the sexist behavior detailed in the complaint wasn’t surprising, according to multiple former employees who spoke on the condition of anonymity in fear of retaliation. Three former employees recounted separate instances in which male authority figures yelled and berated female employees during team meetings, with one of these instances occurring in the past year. Anonymous reviews on job board Glassdoor posted in the last few years echo similar sentiments, with one noting that the company felt like “a glorified good ol' boys club where women are often alienated and ostracized, often unintentionally.” A more extreme review said: “If you aren't a married male who graduated from BYU, then you have no place at this company.”
Two former employees, both of whom worked in Utah for a majority of their careers, said they felt the disrespectful behavior was not “exceptionally bad or very different” within “the bubble of Utah,” citing the state’s predominantly Mormon population, its rigid gender roles and the influence they felt it has had in workplaces where women can often feel ignored, belittled and excluded.
“Pattern takes concerns of this kind seriously,” a company spokesperson wrote to Forbes. “Pattern maintains reporting channels, including anonymous channels, for employees to raise concerns, investigates complaints when they are raised, and acts on findings.”
By the time the lawsuit was settled, Pattern had fully abandoned its short-lived strategy to build brands internally as opposed to fully relying on external customers, ultimately firing or transitioning employees they had acquired or hired for it into different departments. Similar growing pains were felt throughout the company. As Pattern’s strategy moved and changed quickly, allegedly often on Wright’s whim, several departments were subject to what multiple former employees describe as whiplash—characterized internally as “restructurings” involving abrupt layoffs. Two former executives, both of whom were fired, said five executives were let go or departed within the span of a year around 2024, with both recalling that Wright expected fierce loyalty and would be quick to fire when he felt like someone disagreed with him, especially on the direction of the company’s technology. Currently, five of 11 members of the executive team have been in their roles for less than two years. “It’s Dave’s way or the highway,” one former employee said. “Dave has been successful for a reason,” one former executive who was fired said. “The guy's not stupid and he's built up a team of loyal people.”
A Pattern spokesperson denied the characterization that the layoffs were abrupt or that the term “restructuring” was used to obscure their nature. “What matters most is that once we make a decision, the team moves together on it. That is commitment to the business, not to any one person,” Wright wrote to Forbes. “Personnel decisions here are based on performance and results, not on whether someone agreed with me.”
Alder, meanwhile, says she started taking a back seat at the company a few years ago, moving from her chief operating officer role to a strategy officer role in 2018. Multiple former junior-level employees say they rarely saw Alder and that nobody interacted with her on a day-to-day basis, though multiple former executives describe how the couple’s relationship and the fact that they often talked shop at home meant that she was advising him on higher-level decisions, including HR issues. Behind Wright’s decisions at the office, many believe Alder wields enormous influence. “He practically worships her,” one former executive said.
Outsiders may not get it, but Wright and Alder say they couldn't imagine building Pattern anywhere besides Utah. “Work ethic is amazing. The people are very integral and grow up very disciplined from a very young age,” says Wright, who also cites how favorable the state is from a taxes perspective—“conservative culture favors business in many ways.” In fact, U.S. News & World Report ranked Utah as the number one overall best state in the nation this year for a record-breaking fourth consecutive year, thanks to the state's economic growth and opportunities—including its growing tech scene—public infrastructure, and education.
Still, not a single Utah company ranks within the 500 largest public companies in the nation by revenue—and it’s both perplexing and motivating for Wright, who believes Pattern is on the path there. Some critics, like one scathing December 2025 short seller report from financial newsletter The Bear Cave, think Pattern will never get close. The report cited Pattern’s overreliance on Amazon (which represented 93% of its revenue last year), concentration in the health supplement category (69% of its inventory purchases last year) and past failures of Amazon accelerators or aggregators including Pharmapacks—which had surprisingly meaningful revenue growth in the years leading up to its bankruptcy in 2022. Pattern’s stock plummeted 13% the day the report was published last year. The stock has doubled since. (Pattern declined to comment on the report.)
Regardless, it's never been a more exciting time for Wright and Alder. “We're at the intersection of the most significant consumer shift and how they buy—which will be agentic commerce,” Wright says. “There was a time when we thought maybe there would just be a few AI models—OpenAI, Gemini—and I think we're all quickly seeing there's a lot of models out there that are winning, more than we thought.” In a future where customers can directly shop on so many different AI models, Pattern says it will treat those models like new marketplaces—similar to how it figured out TikTok Shop when it surged in popularity. Wright doesn’t detail his plans but calls AI shopping one of Pattern’s biggest opportunities yet.
It’s unclear when shopping on AI models will become the new normal or whether that may even happen, but for now, there’s no shortage of things keeping the cofounders up at night.
results.summary:
Utah-based e-commerce firm Pattern has achieved a $4 billion market valuation by helping brands navigate complex online marketplaces, despite facing internal management scrutiny and intense market competition.

### Key Points
- Founded in 2013 by David Wright and Melanie Alder, Pattern manages online storefronts and logistics for over 200 brands, including Panasonic and Spanx.
- The company generates revenue by purchasing inventory in bulk and selling it across 70 platforms, such as Amazon, TikTok Shop, and Walmart.
- Pattern reported $2.5 billion in revenue last year, with growth exceeding 40% per quarter since its initial public offering.
- The firm has faced allegations of a toxic workplace culture and high executive turnover, which leadership has formally denied.
- Financial critics have raised concerns regarding the company's heavy reliance on Amazon for 93% of its total revenue.

### Why it Matters
Pattern’s rapid ascent highlights the growing demand for specialized intermediaries that can manage the complexities of fragmented digital retail environments. While the company’s stock performance demonstrates strong investor confidence in its AI-driven strategy, its long-term stability remains tied to its ability to diversify beyond Amazon and address internal cultural challenges.

results.title: The Fitness and Recovery Tech I Swear By as a Wellness Expert
results.author: Giselle Castro-Sloboda
results.content:
Using the right fitness and wellness tech can help you to achieve your goals and also help with recovery. As CNET’s resident fitness expert, I’ve tested everything from the best treadmills to smart rings and smart home gyms. As great as some of these products are, there are a few I keep coming back to — and recommending to friends and family. If it’s in your budget and you’re looking to upgrade or improve your workout routine, there are some gadgets I recommend investing in. These are the pieces of tech that you may want to consider to step up your workout and recovery game.
Don’t miss any of our unbiased tech content and lab-based reviews. Add CNET as a preferred Google source on Chrome.
1. Hyperice Normatec Go Boots
The Hyperice Normatec Go compression boots are ideal if you want to recover on the go after a tough workout. These are TSA-friendly so you can travel with them in a carry-on bag or in your gym bag. As a petite woman, the standard Normatec legs tend to be too big on me, so I like that these compression boots are short enough to target the calves. I’ve found it helpful to use them after a run and tough leg day. These are also easily rechargeable and have a 3-hour battery life.
2. Apple Watch Series 11
Although I haven’t had a chance to test the Apple Watch Series 11, I am familiar with the brand and am a loyal Apple Watch owner. The latest version of the Apple Watch has upgraded features like FDA-cleared hypertension alerts, a longer battery life, sleep score and a more scratch-resistant screen. CNET Lead Writer Vanessa Hand Orellana reviewed the smartwatch and said the Series 11 felt like picking up where she left off from the last Apple Watch iteration. Although the Apple Watch already tracked sleep, this is the first time you’ll get quantifiable data that follows clinical guidance to grade your quality of sleep based on sleep duration, bedtime and interruptions.
The stand-out health feature on the Series 11 is the new FDA-cleared hypertension notifications. It tracks your blood pressure and alerts you to potential irregularities. You should double-check this data with a proper blood pressure monitor and your doctor, because the Apple Watch reading isn’t meant to be used as a diagnostic tool.
Another important aspect to highlight is the longer battery life, which helps you enjoy your phone’s features for multiple days before needing to recharge it. This is a great option if you’re looking to upgrade an older Apple Watch model or are new to smartwatches.
3. Theragun Mini 3
The Theragun Mini 3 is tiny yet powerful, and it is a favorite of mine if you want a compact massage gun that packs a mighty punch. Massage guns are helpful to have on hand when you have sore muscles. However, most are on the larger side, so a smaller option is always a good idea.
The Theragun Mini 3 is quieter and lighter than its previous versions and comes with three massage heads (standard ball, dampener and thumb attachments) and a soft carrying case. It’s TSA-friendly and small enough to fit in your purse or backpack. Other factors that make it appealing are that it has three settings and even at its lowest setting, it’s still a powerful device. You can even pair it with the Therabody app to give you recovery plans to follow. You can’t go wrong with a Theragun Mini, whether you’re looking for one for yourself or as a gift for a friend or family member.
4. Theragun PRO Plus
On the other hand, if you’re an athlete putting yourself through tough workouts, the Theragun PRO Plus will quickly become your favorite recovery tool. The Theragun PRO Plus is designed with serious athletes in mind, with various customizable and preset programs, including near-infrared LED light, hot and cold therapy to soothe sore muscles. This heavy-duty massage gun is quieter than the previous model (Theragun PRO-5th Generation) and comes with six attachments, so you’ll get the right angle each time. Additionally, if you want to use the cold therapy function, you’ll need to purchase the PRO Plus cold attachment separately.
If you love to work out hard and take recovery seriously, this massage gun is the best gift you can buy yourself.
5. Oura Ring 5
If you ask me, the Oura Ring is still the best smart ring on the market. It’s most recent version, the Oura Ring 5 quickly won me over because it’s 40% smaller and lighter than the Oura Ring 4. The smart ring tracks your overall health in a holistic manner by gathering your stress levels, heart rate, cycle insights if you menstruate and your sleep. This ring is best known for its ability to track your sleep habits and provide insight to help you improve them based on that data.
The design itself is scratch-resistant, which is a step up from previous models because they would easily get scuffed up. Oura’s original symptom radar, which could detect if you were getting sick, has been updated to be called Health Radar and can detect blood pressure trends. Additionally, if you like to work out, the ring has an automatic workout detection function and can record your workouts. It takes about a month to get the most accurate results, and from there, Oura gives you a readiness score, which tells you how recovered you are, based on sleep and stress levels, to take on the day.
Although it isn’t necessary to own a smart wearable, it’s sometimes helpful to know details about your day-to-day habits that you may be unaware of or how they may be affecting you. For example, as a mom to a toddler, I don’t always get restful sleep, and the Oura Ring was able to detect that and support me as I adjusted my sleep schedule based on its recommendations.
6. Tonal 2
If you’re serious about strength training and have the budget and space in your home, you’ll love owning the Tonal 2. The Tonal 2 is a smart home gym that uses up to 250 pounds of resistance and is designed to replace dumbbells, barbells and other strength-training equipment. It resembles a cable machine with a screen in the middle and adjustable arms on each side.
Tonal 2 uses AI through 13 sensors to track your form and technique, which helps you correct it. Accessories like the smart handles and bar accessories (an optional, additional $495) have a gyroscope motion sensor that also keeps track of your reps. I’ve tested both the Tonal 2 and its predecessor, The Tonal, and was impressed by the thought process that went into designing this machine. It offers strength training as well as some cardio with its new Aero feature, keeps track of your workouts, functions like a personal trainer because it can determine if you need to scale it back or challenge yourself, and also offers thousands of on-demand and live workouts for all fitness levels. The price tag is hefty at $4,295, but if you’re dedicated to strength training and want everything you need at your fingertips, this is the machine for you.
7. Peloton Cross Training Bike Plus
The smart bike that took the fitness world by storm during the COVID-19 pandemic is popular for good reason. I’ve tested many exercise bikes — including Peloton alternatives — and the Peloton is still the best option. In 2025, Peloton overhauled its equipment and introduced its Cross Training Plus line. This included the new Peloton Cross Training Bike Plus, which replaced the Peloton Bike Plus. The latest version of the bike comes with a movement-tracking camera and Peloton IQ — Peloton’s AI coach — which can count reps, correct your form and identify when to increase weights during a strength-training class. Other cosmetic updates include a new seat, a three-speed fan and a phone holder.
Peloton delivers and assembles the bike in your home and sets up your account, so you don’t have to do much but hop on the bike and ride. You can connect with other Peloton members and have friendly competition on the leaderboard. The instructors are high-energy, and each offers something different and motivational to their classes. I’m personally partial to Alex Toussaint and Robin Arzon because every time I take their classes, I’m always inspired to push myself more. Not to mention, Peloton is always revitalizing its workout program offerings (like with kettlebell classes) and challenges, so you won’t ever get bored.
8. Beats Powerbeats Pro 2
I take listening to my music seriously during my workouts. The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are by far some of my favorite earbuds to wear when breaking a sweat. The battery life is impressive and, in my experience, can last for weeks at a time before needing to be recharged. This can vary as it also depends on how often you use them.
The noise-canceling aspect of the Powerbeats Pro 2 is impressive, so your music will always feel immersive whether you’re at the beginning, middle or end of your workout. I’ve also been able to receive phone calls while wearing them, and never had connection issues. I’ve used these earbuds during strength training sessions, outdoor and indoor runs and my daily walks. If you’re looking for a pair of earbuds that stay put (thanks to the ear hook design), have crisp audio and are stylish, these are my top pick.
9. Future Pro app
As a fitness writer, I’ve reviewed a bunch of fitness apps, but one that I particularly enjoyed is the Future Pro app. It’s the ideal app if you’re looking for a virtual personal trainer who can create a workout program for you based on your fitness level and whether you work out at home or the gym.
The app costs $50 a month to start and $199 thereafter. When you sign up, you fill out an assessment intake form, which basically asks you about your goals, workout history, how often you’d like to work out, and what motivates you. Based on your responses, the form offers a selection of trainers to choose from.
I used the Future Pro app for more than a year and loved how well-thought-out and seamless it is. I was paired with a trainer whom I enjoyed checking in with daily through the app chat portal. This app got me through my pregnancy and postpartum period, so I could resume exercising safely. The workouts for the week are shared at the top of the week, and if you need any modifications or if you plan on taking a vacation, the trainer can modify your schedule as needed. The workouts are easy to follow, and the exercises are accompanied by video demonstrations in case you need them for reference. If you want a personal trainer at your fingertips, this is the app to download on your phone.
results.summary:
Top fitness experts recommend a curated selection of high-performance wearable technology, recovery devices, and smart home gym equipment to optimize workout routines and improve overall physical health and recovery.

### Key Points
- **Recovery Tools:** The Hyperice Normatec Go boots offer portable compression, while the Theragun Mini 3 and Theragun PRO Plus provide targeted muscle relief with varying intensity levels.
- **Wearable Tech:** The Apple Watch Series 11 introduces FDA-cleared hypertension alerts, and the Oura Ring 5 features a 40% smaller design with enhanced Health Radar tracking capabilities.
- **Home Fitness:** The Tonal 2 smart gym uses AI-driven sensors for form correction, and the Peloton Cross Training Bike Plus integrates Peloton IQ for real-time rep counting.
- **Audio and Coaching:** Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 earbuds provide immersive noise-canceling audio, while the Future Pro app connects users with virtual personal trainers for customized workout programming.

### Why it Matters
Integrating advanced fitness technology allows users to track biometric data and receive professional-grade guidance that was previously only available in clinical or gym settings. These tools help individuals personalize their recovery and training intensity, leading to more efficient progress toward long-term health and fitness goals.

results.title: I tested the MacBook Neo; now I know why the Googlebook will disappoint
results.author: Jon Gilbert
results.content:
My trusty Chromebook died last week. I'm still unsure exactly what knocked it out of commission, but I knew it was time to let it go. The $300 laptop had served me well for over five years, and it was time for a replacement.
While I was surprised it had lasted me this long, I was hoping it would last me a few more months.
The Googlebook is right around the corner, and it seemed like the ideal replacement. However, now that I've picked up its competitor, I'm glad I didn't wait.
The Googlebook trivia
					challenge
How well do you know Google's hardware history?
					
Think you know everything about the Pixelbook and Google's laptop legacy? Put your knowledge to the test.
What was the name of Google's very first Chromebook, released in 2013 under its own brand?
In what year did Google officially launch the Pixelbook, its rebranded premium laptop successor to the Chromebook Pixel?
Which processor family powered the original 2017 Google Pixelbook?
What unique capability did the 2017 Pixelbook support that was relatively rare for Chromebooks at the time?
What was the name of the stylus accessory designed specifically for the 2017 Google Pixelbook?
What was the name of the smaller, more affordable sibling to the Pixelbook that Google released in 2018?
Google officially discontinued its in-house laptop hardware ambitions in 2023. Which was the last Pixelbook model ever sold?
What operating system powers all Pixelbook and Chromebook Pixel devices made by Google?
Your Score
Thanks for playing!
The more leaks I hear about the Googlebook, the less confident I get
What started as an exciting MacBook competitor has turned into another Gemini product
In March 2026, when rumors around Aluminium OS were heating up, alongside the launch of the MacBook Neo, I became very excited. Finally, a true Android laptop that would bring the iOS/macOS experience to Android devices.
Sure, Android devices sync marvelously with Chromebooks, but no Chromebook can compete with a powerful Windows or macOS laptop. Hence, my excitement for a true competitor to Apple laptops.
However, as the months passed, my excitement waned. Rather than the productivity and media powerhouse I was hoping for, the Googlebook was shaping up to be another way to encourage us to use Gemini.
My opinion didn't improve when I went hands-on with the Magic Cursor demo. Pitched as a flagship feature of the Googlebook, I found it to be clunky, unresponsive, and broken.
August 12 should reveal the Googlebook in full, but it's too late for me.
A week of using the MacBook Neo showed me why the Googlebook will disappoint
Its respectful approach to AI blew me away
I'm a practical man at heart, so I buy the best tools for the job. I needed an affordable laptop that helped me stay productive. Enter the MacBook Neo.
There's a lot I could say about this laptop, but most of it can be summed up by pointing at the price tag. It functions like a laptop twice the price, and has all the bells and whistles one would expect from a MacBook (minus a backlit keyboard, which is annoying).
However, there's one feature that convinced me I had made the right choice.
While setting up my MacBook Neo, I was asked if I wanted to use Apple Intelligence. I cheerfully clicked "No" and continued on my way.
A week later, I noticed something. Or rather, the lack of something. Not once had I seen a pop-up, suggestion, or reminder to use Apple Intelligence.
I know I won't get this level of respect from a Googlebook
Google won't let you ignore its flagship feature
It might seem silly to point out that after confirming that I didn't want to use Apple Intelligence, I didn't see the feature again.
However, my experience with Gemini over the years is that Google doesn't take "no" for an answer.
Yes, I can disable the Gemini app and uninstall the AI Core app, but Gemini is everywhere. It's baked into Chrome, Google Search, and apps like Gmail and Drive. I can't use the Google ecosystem without seeing Gemini.
By contrast, after disabling Apple Intelligence, I never saw it again. I've hunted through all the preinstalled apps on my MacBook Neo, including Siri, and I haven't come across hide nor hair of it.
Apple Intelligence is still in beta, so there's still a chance Apple can follow the Google route. But using this laptop is a breath of fresh air and the distinct sense that I've dodged a bullet.
Baking AI into hardware is a consumer-unfriendly decision
Google is banking on people wanting a dedicated Gemini machine
I have no particular desire to use Apple Intelligence, but if I change my mind, it's only a settings toggle away.
That's what the AI experience should be. I use a few AI tools infrequently, and I'm grateful for them. But like any tool, I like to put them away when done.
I use a screwdriver about once a month, but if Google provided it, it would check in every day to see if I needed it. I know when I need to use a screwdriver. I know when I need an AI tool; I don't need to be reminded about it.
The problem is that Google has bet so big on AI that it has to push it on everything to avoid disaster. Apple, on the other hand, seems content to develop AI as just another tool.
The result is an experience where I'm in control of AI. On a Googlebook, I won't get that level of respect.
Google is going to struggle to make the Googlebook succeed
Even if the Googlebook wasn't a Gemini-first product, I would still be apprehensive about its future.
It's going to be hard to ditch the legacy of Chromebooks, and people will be reluctant to give up the Windows and macOS laptops they've grown used to for years.
Chromebook users are the best target, but is shoving Gemini in their faces the best way to encourage an upgrade? I don't think so.
If Google really wants to mimic Apple's success, it needs to take the same consumer-friendly approach to AI.
results.summary:
Anticipation for the upcoming Googlebook has waned as reports suggest the device will prioritize aggressive Gemini AI integration over the user-controlled experience offered by competing laptop platforms.

### Key Points
- The Googlebook is scheduled for a full reveal on August 12, following years of Google hardware development including the Pixelbook series.
- Early demonstrations of the "Magic Cursor" feature have been criticized for being unresponsive and clunky during hands-on testing.
- Unlike Apple’s approach with Apple Intelligence, which allows users to opt out entirely, Google integrates Gemini across its entire software ecosystem.
- The author opted for a MacBook Neo, citing a preference for hardware that does not force persistent AI suggestions or reminders on the user.
- Google officially discontinued its previous in-house laptop hardware line in 2023, ending the legacy of the Pixelbook.

### Why it Matters
The shift toward "AI-first" hardware design highlights a growing divide in how major tech companies approach consumer autonomy and software integration. Users are increasingly prioritizing devices that offer control over AI features, potentially creating a market disadvantage for products that mandate constant engagement with generative tools.

results.title: Foldable 'iPhone Ultra 3' Rumored to Feature Larger Displays
results.author: Hartley Charlton
results.content:
Apple is already making plans for its third-generation foldable iPhone, with launch expected as early as 2028, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
Writing in his latest "Power On" newsletter, Gurman said the first foldable iPhone is about to get what he called the device's first "truly revolutionary design change" this year, and that Apple already has a roadmap extending two generations beyond it. A second-generation model is planned for 2027, Gurman says, with a third version following as early as 2028.
The third-generation foldable will apparently feature slightly larger displays on both the inside and the outside compared to its predecessors, though he did not provide specific screen sizes. The first foldable iPhone is expected to launch with a 7.8-inch inner display and a 5.5-inch cover display, so any increase would build on those dimensions. This is the first report to lay out plans for a third-generation model, extending Apple's foldable roadmap a year beyond where it previously stood.
The first foldable iPhone is expected to arrive this year with an ultra-thin design, Touch ID instead of Face ID, the A20 chip, C2 modem, and the moniker "iPhone Ultra," at a price around or above $2,000. The second-generation foldable, meanwhile, is reported to have already received the go-ahead for development, according to the Weibo leaker known as "Digital Chat Station," who said the "iPhone Ultra 2" project has been formally approved and will likely reuse the first-generation model's display. That model is expected to launch in fall 2027 alongside the 20th-anniversary iPhone.
results.summary:
Apple is reportedly developing a third-generation foldable iPhone for a potential 2028 release, expanding its long-term hardware roadmap to include larger displays and iterative design improvements over time.

### Key Points
- Apple plans to launch its first foldable iPhone this year, featuring a 7.8-inch inner display, an A20 chip, and a price point starting around $2,000.
- The second-generation "iPhone Ultra 2" is officially in development and is currently scheduled for a fall 2027 release alongside the 20th-anniversary iPhone.
- A third-generation foldable model is projected for 2028, with early reports indicating it will feature larger internal and external screen dimensions than its predecessors.
- The initial foldable device will reportedly prioritize an ultra-thin design and utilize Touch ID instead of the standard Face ID authentication system.

### Why it Matters
This extended roadmap signals Apple's commitment to establishing a long-term presence in the competitive foldable smartphone market. By planning three generations of hardware, the company aims to refine its foldable technology and maintain its premium market position against established rivals.

results.title: Made by Google 2026 Launch Live: Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Pixel Watch 5, Gemini, and all the news
results.author: derrek.lee@futurenet.com (Derrek Lee) , Derrek Lee
results.content:
Google is back this year with its Made by Google event, and we’re expecting a lot of Pixel news. Of course, Google is set to launch the Pixel 11 series, which will likely include several different smartphones as well as a new foldable. In addition, Google is expected to launch the Pixel Watch 5, and there could be some additional devices in the mix.
We hope you’re as excited to learn about Google’s latest smartphones as we are! Last year’s launch was filled with celebrities and internet personalities, and this year looks to be no different, with Stephen Curry, Shubman Gill, Ayami Nakajo, and more, with Trevor Noah hosting.
Over the next few days, we’ll be going over what you can expect and covering the event live as it happens so you don’t have to miss a thing! Scroll down for all the details!
When and what time is Made by Google?
The event is Wednesday, August 12, and it starts at 3 p.m. PT / 6 p.m. EDT.
How to watch the Made by Google event?
Google will stream the event on its official Made by Google YouTube Channel. You can also watch it live at the Google Store website. Click the Notify Me button below so you don’t miss a thing!
While Derrek might be disappointed in the rumor that the Pixel Watch 5 isn't going to use the new Snapdragon Wear Elite chipset, I'm actually quite happy to hear this news. I've (Nick Sutrich) been using the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for the past two weeks, which uses that new Snapdragon Wear Elite chipset, and the battery life is comparatively awful compared to any other recent Snapdragon Wear chip I've gotten my hands on.
The W5 series, by comparison, seems to have a much better performance efficiency balance than Qualcomm's newest supercharged chip. Considering all the Pixel Watch models powered by Snapdragon still feel snappy to this day, I'd much rather stick with this more efficient chipset line than something that's unnecessarily more powerful.
One change I’m hoping to see with the Pixel Watch 5 is an upgrade to the fitness tracking. Garmin is my go-to for fitness because it can set detailed workout routines and track reps and sets. As someone who frequents the gym and lifts weights, this is incredibly useful to me, and the reason why I switch out my Pixel Watch for the Garmin Venu 4 when I work out. If the Pixel Watch 5 can get this right, I can probably just stick to one smartwatch going forward. That said, I won’t get my hopes up.
Speaking of keeping costs down, it looks like even Google won’t be able to avoid the inevitable price increase with the Pixel Watch 5. One rumor points to Google increasing the base price by $50, bringing it to a starting price of $399 for the 41mm variant. Would you pay that much for a smartwatch?
I’m also excited to see what’s coming with the Pixel Watch 5. Based on Google’s teaser, it won’t look much different from the Pixel Watch 4, which has been one of my favorite smartwatches in the past year. However, early rumors suggest there also won’t be a change in chipset, while more recent rumors suggest it’ll feature an “Accelerated” version of the Snapdragon W5 Gen 2. It’s a bummer that it may not feature the premium “Snapdragon Wear Elite” found in the new Galaxy Watch 9 and Ultra 2, but last year’s chip was no slouch, and it’s likely this is to help keep costs down while providing more AI capabilities.
I’ve (Derrek Lee) been using the base Pixel 10 for about a year, and it’s quite a step-up from the Pixel 9. The cameras are phenomenal, and I love the Qi2 support since it doesn’t force me to put a case on this already thick phone.
I’m curious how the Pixel 11 will upgrade the base Pixel experience, perhaps with more base storage and faster charging?
It would also be nice if Google made the Pixel 11 a bit thinner, perhaps by giving it a denser silicon-carbon battery… but I won’t get my hopes up.
Chromebooks have dominated classrooms over the last decade, and it is a bold bet by Google to switch things up with the Googlebook. The high-end hardware combined with tight-knit integration with Gemini is interesting, but Google is going up against a well-established Windows ecosystem and MacBooks. I guess we’ll have to wait and see where the initial batch of Googlebooks slot in; that will give us a good idea as to what Google is planning to get out of its latest product category.
The defining feature of the Googlebook is the Magic Pointer, where you can easily get contextual information from Gemini just by wiggling your cursor at whatever you're browsing. This is what Google says when it's talking about Gemini Intelligence being integral to the Googlebook, and I'm very excited to see how it holds up in daily use.
What's notable with the Googlebook is that it could showcase what Android and ChromeOS can do together. Google is going about this the right way, with major hardware vendors slated to release Googlebooks later in the year. The software will ultimately prove to be the defining factor, and I think there's definitely potential to see how Google brings Android and ChromeOS together into a unified ecosystem.
Returning to highlights of The Android Show, the Googlebook teaser got everyone excited about how Google will deliver the Chromebook successor. What stands out this time is that the Googlebook is aimed as a high-end device, with Google noting that it puts Gemini front and center. We'll also get a mix of regular x86-based models and Arm devices, and I'm interested in the latter — there's much better battery life with Arm notebooks in general, and I can't wait to see how Google utilizes this with the Googlebook.
What I like the most in Android 17 is the Bubbles multitasking mode. The ability to use floating windows allows much greater flexibility, and it makes a lot of sense on a foldable like the Pixel 10 Pro Fold. There's better fluidity in general with the interface, and this was a phoe problem in the past.
Samsung also joined the Android 17 bandwagon with its foldables, and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 models come with One UI 9.0 and the latest version of Android out of the box. Of course, Samsung's vision of Android looks very different to what Google has on the Pixels, and that's one of the best things about Android; you can choose what kind of interface you want on your phone. On that note, other brands are starting to roll out the stable Android 17 update to their phones, with Xiaomi getting us underway.
One of the main reasons why Google pushed the Android release ahead last year is to ensure its latest devices get the latest build of the OS out of the box. With Google releasing phones in August and subsequently rolling out a new Android version in the month of October didn't really make much sense, so it's good to see Android builds coming out earlier. The stable Android 17 version was released on June 16, and Google's eligible devices have made the switch already.
Be honest: Android Auto has been lacking, right? If you’re asking me, I’d say “kind of.” Google has continued to improve Android Auto over the years. Gemini’s involvement has helped, too. At the Android Show, Android Auto was shown with a vastly improved, “immersive” Google Maps experience with an edge-to-edge display, and a robust 3D view. Android Auto will tell you what you should keep an eye out for, like traffic lights and lanes. It’s no longer generic. It’s actually helpful.
Since we’re now, officially, in the second half of 2026, we should start seeing Google’s upgraded Live Threat Detection. This will deliver “warnings about suspicious behavior that could be potentially harmful.” Take, for example, an app trying to force a text message to another number you don’t know. The idea is to ward off malicious trickery, and there’s a chance we’ll see this talked about with the Pixel 11’s launch.
Another Android upgrade Google gave us—in line with its recent behavior—involved scam protections. At the Android Show 2026, Google talked about protections for your banking apps by introducing “verified financial calls.” We work hard for our money. The last thing we want is for it to get swiped. If Google deems that call to be a fraud, it will tell you to hang up now.
While we wait for Made by Google, why not have a little to snack on? The Android Show this year talked up the company’s security improvements. One of the major highlights was Location Access. I know, I thought the same thing. Google made this more transparent so we can manage how an app accesses our location, and when it happened. We don’t always want to put ourselves out there like that, so I like that Google worked this into Android.
Another Android 17 feature I'm really looking forward to is Rambler. I've talked about it before, but it's essentially Google's new AI-powered voice typing system. Instead of speaking carefully and trying not to make mistakes, you can just talk naturally. Rambler automatically ignores your "ums" and "ahs," understands corrections as you speak, and turns everything into properly formatted text. It's very similar to what we've recently seen with Gemini on macOS, but this time it's coming to Android smartphones. That's one of the Android 17 features I'm probably most excited to try.
Speaking of the Pixel launch event, as a Pixel 10 Pro owner, I'm honestly not that excited about the Pixel 11 series itself. Based on everything we've seen so far, there don't seem to be many major hardware upgrades this year. What I'm actually looking forward to is Android 17 and the new features launching alongside the Pixel 11.One feature I'm especially excited about is the new 3D emojis. Google first showed them off during The Android Show, but we still haven't seen them arrive on Pixel phones. They're still not quite on the same level as Apple's emoji design, in my opinion, but they're definitely a big improvement over what Android has today.
Speaking of Googlebook, Google has been unusually quiet about it ever since The Android Show. That makes me wonder whether the upcoming Made by Google event could finally give us a proper look at Google's next-generation premium laptops. What do you think? Do you expect Googlebook to make an appearance next week? Let me know in the comments.
Since we're looking back at The Android Show from earlier this year, it's worth remembering that it was actually the first time Google quietly gave us a look at what is now rumored to be called Pixel Glow, or HiLight.
During the Googlebook teaser, you could spot a glowing light bar across the top of the laptop lid. Since then, we've seen the same design language appear on the new Google Home Speaker, and according to recent leaks, it's also expected to make its way to the Pixel 11 series.
One of the other Gemini highlights from The Android Show 2026 was the new Create A Widget feature, which turns Gemini into a professional coder so you can make custom home screen widgets. Nothing started this trend a few months ago and did a spectacular job with the implementation, and I expect to see Google take the concept even further on the Pixel 11.
The concept is pretty simple. Say you want a specific widget that doesn't seem to exist in the Play Store. Just ask Gemini to create a widget for you, and it'll begin the coding process, complete with the ability to revise and modify things as the widget is being built.
For me, the most interesting part of Gemini Intelligence and automation is when Gemini is used to interact with apps that aren't usually deemed "compatible." Let's say you're particularly find of an obscure note app that wouldn't normally have tie-ins with services like Gemini. No problem, because Gemini Intelligence is supposed to be able to work with it, regardless.
Say you took a photo of a banner or poster for an upcoming event and want to make a shopping list based on what you'll need for it. Gemini can help navigate the content in the photo and fill out a note in your favorite app without you manually typing it in. That's just one of many features we're expecting to see expanded on the new Pixel 11 series, too!
Google was already in the midst of doing some heavy brand reworking with Gemini, and Android 17 only furthers those actions. Google says that Android is no longer an "operating system" but, rather, an "intelligence system." This sounds like marketing nonsense, and I'm some of it certainly is, but the idea is that Android is moving beyond a traditional point-and-click (or tap) UI and, instead, becoming a system that does exactly what you ask of it.
Case in point, the newer Gemini Automation features which will navigate entire apps and websites for you with a single command. I used it to order food and tea from two different restaurants and all I had to do was hit confirm. While I'd argue that having Gemini order food for me is silly and completely unnecessary, seeing Gemini have the ability to navigate complex UIs without error is impressive, and there will no doubt be more sensible reasons to use this feature in the near future.
Android 17 is shaping up to be a more social-media-focused update, and on the other side of Pause Point, the company launched Screen Reactions, which makes it incredibly easy to record yourself over another video. It’s an incredibly useful feature and very easy to use. It makes me wonder what other social features the Pixel 11 will introduce.
Another feature I hope to see on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is the Gamepad. It basically turns your foldable into a mini game console of sorts with a dedicated control pad on the bottom half of the screen, which should enhance the gaming experience. Google also says it will include native controller remapping for those of you who use external controllers, which is a great way to appeal to mobile gamers.
One feature I can’t wait to get my hands on is Pause Point. It’s supposed to remind you to take a break from distracting apps with things like timers, breathing exercises, and even suggestions for less-distracting apps to use. Because we all need a reminder to take a break from social media, right? It’s actually a pretty thoughtful feature, one I never expected from Google.
Google has been low-key hyping up its Pixel 11 series for some time, although we just didn’t know it. Earlier this year, the company gave us a glimpse of new features arriving with Android 17, and while the update is already out, there are still some features that haven’t arrived yet, and likely more that Google hasn’t even teased. What are you looking forward to the most?

results.title: ⁠Is ICE using too much force? New poll shows big public opinion shift
results.author: Christopher Cann, USA TODAY
results.content:
Is ICE using too much force? New poll shows big public opinion shift
Months of immigration enforcement controversies have taken their toll, and new polling shows it could be a problem for Republicans heading into the midterms.
About 8 in 10 independent voters say U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has used too much force in its nationwide operations, according to a poll from YouGov, which sampled 1,000 voters in late July. It's a striking increase from 2025, when polls showed independents more divided on the issue.
The poll, commissioned by the Vera Institute of Justice, a nonprofit working to end mass incarceration, was conducted shortly after ICE officers shot and killed two immigrants during traffic stops in Maine and Texas over the span of six days in July.
An earlier YouGov poll, which was conducted before the two shootings, found that most independents – 62% – believe ICE has gone too far. Other polls from YouGov, AP-NORC and The Civic Health and Institutions Project found that only a fraction of independent voters support ICE's handling of immigration enforcement.
The data comes months ahead of the midterms, as Republicans are seeking to hold onto a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. Several races are expected to be close and could be decided by independent voters – a group whose support has grown increasingly vital in recent elections.
The Department of Homeland Security in an emailed statement cited June polling data showing 80% of Americans support "deporting immigrants who are here illegally and have committed crimes.” The statement urged cities to cooperate with ICE and praised the work of immigration officers.
Immigration was one of the top issues that led Republicans to win the presidency and gain full control of Congress in 2024, amid mounting frustrations over the Biden administration's handling of the U.S. southern border. But high-profile enforcement raids and multiple deadly shootings over the last year have eroded support for a central part of President Donald Trump's immigration agenda, political scientists and strategists said.
But not all of the president's actions on immigration are as unpopular as ICE's interior enforcement. The plunging number of border crossings into the United States is considered a success among at least half of all Americans, including independents, polls show. And Republicans overall maintain a sizable advantage on which party voters believe would do a better job at handling border security.
But with the midterms less than three months away, any uptick in disfavor for ICE among independents could spell trouble for Republicans seeking to win over voters from the center, experts said.
“This is a big vulnerability,” said Matthew Grossman, a political scientist and professor of public policy at Michigan State University. “An issue that [Republicans] had in previous elections is now working to their disadvantage.”
In a statement, National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Mike Marinella said GOP candidates running in the midterms will continue to embrace Trump's record on immigration and draw a contrast with the Biden administration.
“President Trump secured the border and is finally enforcing the law after four years of Biden-Harris chaos that let fentanyl and criminals pour into this country and cost American lives in every district," he said. "Democrats spent four years defending open borders and calling it compassion while Americans paid the price. Republicans will keep drawing that contrast in every district, because voters haven’t forgotten what lawlessness looks like.”
'The public mood has changed'
Trump was elected with a promise to carry out the largest deportation operation in U.S. history. On the campaign trail, his supporters held signs that read “MASS DEPORTATION NOW!” And in a 2024 interview with Time magazine, Trump said he wanted to deport “probably 15 million and maybe as many as 20 million” people.
Polls conducted in the months before the 2024 election saw Trump leading Biden by roughly 20 points on immigration and border security. Some polls found that for most voters, immigration was their top issue.
But controversies have eroded that support.
Surges of federal agents into cities such as Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis fueled mass protests, lawsuits and widespread claims of harassment and racial profiling. In January, public outrage spiked following the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good by immigration officers in Minnesota.
In the aftermath, immigration authorities sought to keep a lower profile, moving away from the highly visible raids that drew intense scrutiny. Republicans, meanwhile, talked less about mass deportations and more about targeted enforcement going after criminals, as well as the low number of border crossings.
But protests and backlash reignited again in July after ICE agents in Texas and Maine shot and killed two men in less than a week. And while immigration authorities have largely halted their high-profile raids, ICE detentions have surged.
A poll from The Associated Press and NORC conducted after the shootings found that 39% of adults approved of Trump’s performance on immigration, down from 49% at the start of his term.
According to the same poll, 3 in 10 adults approve of the way ICE is enforcing immigration laws. Among independents, 18% approved of ICE’s actions.
“This has consequences for the campaigns,” said Kyle Kondik, a political analyst who has written several books on U.S. elections. “Some of the messaging that Republicans thought was effective in 2024 on immigration may not be anymore because the public mood has changed.”
Immigration remains a deeply partisan issue
Polls show that views on immigration largely fall along party lines, as has been the trend for more than a decade, experts said.
Less than 2 in 10 Republicans say ICE has used excessive force, and most either said the agency has used “about the right amount of force” or “not enough,” according to the YouGov poll conducted in July. Democrats, meanwhile, remain firmly opposed to the immigration enforcement operations underway, with 9 in 10 saying ICE has gone too far.
In primary races across the United States, immigration was one of the central issues in campaign speeches and advertisements, especially in areas that saw large amounts of enforcement actions.
Some Democratic candidates who won their party’s nomination have called for ICE to be abolished, including progressives in Michigan, Illinois and New Jersey.
On the Republican side, many primary candidates leaned into immigration, spending tens of millions on advertisements that mention or were solely focused on the issue, according to data from the firm AdImpact. Those in areas that have seen controversial ICE actions have walked a tightrope, criticizing some tactics while supporting popular immigration-related initiatives like enhanced border security.
It’s largely proved successful. On Aug. 4, a slate of Trump-backed Republican candidates who support the administration’s immigration enforcement efforts won the GOP nomination in Washington state, Kansas and Michigan.
But, as analysts note, candidates often appeal to their party's hard-line or most vocal factions in primaries before later tempering their messages.
“They’re speaking to a different electorate in the primary than they are in the general,” Grossman said.
What does this mean for the midterms?
It’s unclear how much of an impact immigration will have on the November elections, analysts said. A lot can happen by the time voters head to the polls. And in each district, voters’ priorities are different.
The YouGov poll conducted in late June and early July found that cost of living, inflation and the economy were the top issues for voters – not immigration, which ranked below healthcare policy and international military conflicts. Recent polling from Pew Research Center and Marquette Law School showed similar results.
But like immigration, public support for Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war has waned, giving Republican candidates limited options for a positive messaging strategy heading into November, analysts said.
Experts suspect Republican candidates will focus their messaging on their opponents in coming months.
“Their current positive sign, as [Republicans] see it, is Democrats are nominating more extreme candidates,” Grossman said, speaking about the wave of progressives who’ve won Democratic primaries across the country. “That might mean more negative campaigns going into the fall.”
GOP leadership has already begun employing this tactic.
During an Aug. 5 speech focused on the economy and how his policies have lowered costs for Americans, Trump repeatedly turned to the progressive wing of the Democratic Party.
“These people are dangerous and, frankly, lunatics,” Trump told the crowd at a Las Vegas casino. “They’re crazy, and we can’t let them get into office.”
Christopher Cann is a national reporter for USA TODAY. Contact him by email at ccann@usatoday.com.
results.summary:
A new YouGov poll reveals that 80% of independent voters believe ICE uses excessive force, potentially creating a significant political vulnerability for Republicans ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.

### Key Points
- A July YouGov survey of 1,000 voters found that 80% of independents believe ICE employs excessive force during enforcement operations.
- Public sentiment shifted significantly following two fatal shootings of immigrants by ICE officers in Maine and Texas during July.
- Approval of President Trump’s handling of immigration dropped to 39% in recent AP-NORC polling, down from 49% earlier in his term.
- While interior enforcement faces backlash, approximately half of Americans continue to view the reduction in border crossings as a success.
- Republicans maintain a polling advantage on general border security, despite the growing controversy surrounding specific ICE tactics.

### Why it Matters
The erosion of support among independent voters could jeopardize Republican efforts to maintain their narrow congressional majorities in the upcoming midterms. As immigration enforcement becomes a liability, GOP candidates may struggle to balance their hard-line platform with the shifting priorities of moderate voters.

results.title: These AI Barons Are Ready to Give Away Their Fortunes
results.author: Joel Khalili
results.content:
David Silver is a billionaire, sort of. His stake in Ineffable Intelligence—the artificial intelligence lab he founded—is worth an ungodly fortune. But he stands to collect none of that money himself. He set things up that way.
Between 2013 and 2025, Silver worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He specialized in reinforcement learning, a method of teaching an AI model through positive and negative feedback. In 2016, he led the development of AlphaGo, which became the first AI to defeat a human champion in the game of Go and was heralded as a narrow form of superintelligence. Silver left to start Ineffable Intelligence in January, betting that reinforcement learning breakthroughs will close the gap between human and machine cognition across the board.
When he started Ineffable Intelligence, Silver raised $1.1 billion from investors at a $5.1 billion valuation, reportedly the largest seed round in Europe’s history. He also vowed to donate all the money he makes from any future sale of his company to charity.
“I was thinking very deeply about what I could do to have the maximum impact on the world,” Silver tells WIRED in an interview at his office in Kings Cross, London, around the corner from DeepMind’s headquarters. “Not just through the work I do, but through the finance I arrive at in the process.”
He’ll choose how to deploy the funds after he sells his company, he says, but his ambition is to save as many lives as possible.
Silver is the latest in a growing line of AI founders to pledge equity proceeds to charity. Others include Mustafa Suleyman, a DeepMind cofounder and the CEO of AI at Microsoft, and Anton Osika, the founder of automated coding platform Lovable. If OpenAI and Anthropic go public as planned, minting thousands of new millionaires in the process, the AI industry could soon come to represent an increasingly outsize proportion of tech philanthropy.
Along with a new generation of techno-philanthropists, though, comes a tangle of unresolved questions: Is philanthropy the most appropriate way to redistribute wealth? To what degree are megadonors responsible for some of the problems they aim to fix? Could a pledge that scales with a company’s success come to justify unsavory business practices or reckless accelerationism? And is this go-around any different from previous iterations of Silicon Valley giving?
“You can’t necessarily appeal to capitalism to solve some of the problems created by capitalist practices themselves … the exacerbation of extreme wealth concentration and massive inequalities,” says Linsey McGoey, professor of sociology at the University of Essex and author of No Such Thing as a Free Gift. “It’s like calling upon the arsonist to hose down the house he’s just set on fire.”
Silver formalized his charitable commitment through Founders Pledge, a nonprofit that helps entrepreneurs to give away their wealth. Unlike the Giving Pledge, a public but nonbinding commitment, Founders Pledge requires participants to enter into a contract. “The choice of making a binding pledge was very important,” says Silver.
Founders Pledge has been around since 2015. But the value of pledges recorded by the nonprofit has soared recently, from $400 million in 2023 to $4 billion so far this year. The AI industry now accounts for a third of the lifetime pledge total.
The organization’s goal, according to cofounder David Goldberg, is to identify “the very best ways to deploy capital at scale to make the world better.” It has frequently been lumped together with effective altruism, which encourages people to amass wealth in order to give it away, to rely on statistics rather than emotion, and to prioritize causes likely to have the biggest impact in the distant future. But despite the commonalities, Goldberg isn’t a fan of the comparison; Founders Pledge is concerned with human suffering in the present. “We’re far more humanist,” he says.
Silver considers himself an effective altruist but says his “flavor is about the here and now.” Accordingly, Silver plans to funnel his pledge proceeds to charities, like the Malaria Foundation, equipped to save the greatest number of lives in the near term. “I find it hard to justify focusing on the galactic future of humanity when there are millions of people suffering and dying today,” he says.
Osika, the Lovable founder, who has pledged to give away half of his equity proceeds, doesn’t identify as an effective altruist, but he shares the belief that amassing wealth by succeeding in business is the best way for him to maximize his personal impact on the world. “I think it’s a very good thing for people who are very thoughtful about the future of humanity to build [AI],” he tells WIRED.
The Gates Foundation—the most famous embodiment of techno-philanthropy—has given away more than $100 billion to causes targeting poverty and disease in the 25 years since it was founded by Bill and Melinda Gates. Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have pledged to donate their $200 billion fortune to scientific research through their own foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. Both have been held up as shining examples of how an entrepreneurial mindset can translate into effective philanthropy and how the profit motive can be harnessed for good.
The new generation of AI philanthropists appear to want to carry that legacy forward, into a world they imagine will be utterly reorganized by superintelligence. “For a very long time, it’s been clear to me that this technological transformation is going to be the biggest thing that happens in our lives,” says Osika.
However, this type of giving can come with trade-offs, and can be used by megadonors to discreetly advance their political interests, McGoey says. A recent study found that a reliance on philanthropic funding led the WHO to prioritize donors’ preferred causes at the expense of other urgent issues, like non-communicable diseases.
Donations that alleviate issues stemming from wealth inequality instead of attacking the root cause, McGoey argues, threaten to end the debate about long-term, systemic remedies before it begins. “It’s appealing to the perpetuator of a problem to resolve it—and that doesn’t necessarily lead to positive results,” she says. “I don’t think that people should kid themselves that making money on its own is somehow noble.”
The WHO itself has acknowledged issues with its financing, and in 2022 it put forth a new model designed to address some of those concerns. Mark Suzman, the Gates Foundation’s CEO, has also recognized the pitfalls of relying on megadonors. “It’s not right for a private philanthropy to be one of the largest funders of multinational global health efforts,” he said in 2023, noting that the foundation had become the WHO’s second-largest donor. But he also put the blame on dwindling governmental contributions. “I’d love it if many more governments would pass us on that list,” he said.
Megadonors can play a valuable role in funding causes neglected for ideological reasons by governments, like family planning. But they’re not equally accountable, says Apolline Taillandier, a researcher at the University of Cambridge who specializes in political theory. “These funders are not elected. They have no need to account for their decisions,” she says. “It comes down to the question of whether philanthropy is the most legitimate way of redistributing resources.”
There is a further risk that entrepreneurs might treat their philanthropic ambition as moral justification for destructive behavior. In 2024, the one-time crypto kingpin and effective altruism poster boy Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud. At trial, a former colleague testified that Bankman-Fried had based all of his decisions on cold statistical analysis, gladly risking disaster if it meant a chance at a sufficiently positive end result. The leaders of effective altruism declared Bankman-Friend an apostate, but others painted his fraud as a symptom of the movement's flawed moral logic.
In the context of artificial intelligence, the concern is that a charitable pledge could form part of a risk calculation. By Bankman-Friedian logic, the headlong pursuit of superintelligence would be justified, potential consequences be damned, if the money it creates will have a large enough philanthropic impact.
Silver denies that his pledge is part of some sort of moral accounting or a hedge against the possible negative outcomes of the AI race. He believes that superintelligence will have a radically positive impact, endlessly discovering new knowledge through a recursive cycle of trial and error.
Far from justifying reckless accelerationism, Silver argues, a pledge helps to eliminate the type of financial incentive that threatens to lead AI development astray. “Building a superintelligence company is a huge responsibility to the planet, and that responsibility shouldn’t be led by personal greed,” says Silver. “This was an intentional choice to make sure that whatever actions I take as an individual are for the benefit of humanity, not because there’s some enormous dollar figure that starts to appear on the horizon.”
Silver may be a beneficiary of an economic system stacked in his favor. But one of few ways he can redress that imbalance, he argues, is to give his money away. “Individuals that choose to use their money for good will have a massive, transformative difference on the future of the world we live in,” he says. “That’s independent of whether the macroeconomic situation is the right thing for humanity. It’s just a fact.”
